lesson.title: Adding Functions, Adding Derivatives: The Sum Rule
lesson.summary: The sum rule states that the derivative of a sum of two functions equals the sum of their derivatives, a direct consequence of how limits distribute over addition.
lesson.body:
When two functions are added together to form a new function, it would be convenient if you could just differentiate each piece separately and add the results. The sum rule confirms that this convenient shortcut is exactly correct: if f and g are both differentiable, then the derivative of f(x) + g(x) is f'(x) + g'(x). There is no interaction term, no correction factor, nothing extra to worry about, addition of functions really is that well behaved under differentiation.

To see why, apply the limit definition to the sum function directly. Let k(x) = f(x) + g(x). Then k(x+h) = f(x+h) + g(x+h), so the difference quotient is [k(x+h) - k(x)] / h = [f(x+h) + g(x+h) - f(x) - g(x)] / h. Regrouping the numerator by which original function each term came from gives [f(x+h) - f(x)] + [g(x+h) - g(x)], all still divided by h. Since division distributes over addition, this splits into [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h + [g(x+h) - g(x)] / h. Now take the limit as h approaches 0. Because limits of sums equal sums of limits, whenever each individual limit exists, this becomes the limit of the first difference quotient plus the limit of the second, which is exactly f'(x) + g'(x). That completes the proof: k'(x) = f'(x) + g'(x).

For a worked example, let f(x) = x^3 and g(x) = x^2, and consider their sum, k(x) = x^3 + x^2. By the power rule, f'(x) = 3x^2 and g'(x) = 2x. The sum rule then says k'(x) = 3x^2 + 2x, without needing to expand any limit for the combined function directly. Check this at x = 2: k'(2) = 3(2)^2 + 2(2) = 3(4) + 4 = 12 + 4 = 16. You can verify this matches computing each piece's derivative at x = 2 separately and adding: f'(2) = 3(4) = 12, g'(2) = 2(2) = 4, and 12 + 4 = 16, the same answer.

This rule is what makes it reasonable to differentiate a polynomial term by term instead of treating the whole expression as one indivisible block inside a single limit computation. Each power of x contributes its own derivative via the power rule, and the sum rule guarantees those contributions simply add up with nothing lost or gained in the process.

The sum rule extends naturally beyond just two functions: since f + g + k can be grouped as (f + g) + k, applying the two-function sum rule twice shows that the derivative of any finite sum of differentiable functions equals the sum of their individual derivatives. This generalization will be used constantly once polynomials with many terms are differentiated all at once, later in this same sequence of chapters.

Notice that the sum rule proof leaned on a limit law rather than any brand new algebra: the statement that a limit of a sum equals the sum of the limits, provided each limit exists on its own. This is the same limit machinery that underlies the derivative definition itself, so the sum rule is really a structural consequence of how limits behave, not a coincidence specific to derivatives. This also explains why the rule places no restriction on what f and g actually are, beyond both being differentiable at the point in question: the argument never used any special property of polynomials, roots, or any other specific family of functions, so it applies just as well once you meet trigonometric, exponential, or logarithmic functions in later coursework.
